[THOUGHT] The patient is a 34‑year‑old with multiple bilateral lesions of the lower eyelid region that have been slowly increasing over several years. Although detailed lesion descriptors are lacking, the location (lower eyelids), multiplicity, bilateral symmetry, and slow progressive course strongly favor benign adnexal tumors of eccrine origin — classically syringomas. Syringomas commonly present as multiple small (1–3 mm), flesh‑colored to yellowish papules clustered on the lower eyelids in young adults, more often women, and progress slowly. Milia (tiny white keratin cysts) can appear around the eyes but are usually whitish, often smaller and more transient or treated easily; they are less classically multiple, symmetric and progressively enlarging over years. Xanthelasma typically presents as soft yellow plaques on the medial eyelids and is associated with hyperlipidemia (though lipids can be normal); the plaque morphology and usual location differ from the typical syringoma appearance. Given the age, bilateral lower‑eyelid location, multiplicity, and chronic slow growth, syringomas are the single most likely diagnosis.

[DIAGNOSIS] Syringomas (multiple periorbital eccrine sweat‑gland adenomas)

Important "red flags" that would change urgency or differential — rapid growth, bleeding/ulceration, visual changes, systemic symptoms — are not documented. Critical diagnostic information is missing: no physical exam descriptors (size, color, number, morphology, texture), no clinical photos, no dermoscopy or histology, and no exact lipid values (only reported as "normal"). A normal fasting lipid panel argues against xanthelasma but does not confirm syringomas. Because syringomas are a clinical-histologic diagnosis, confirmation generally requires at minimum characteristic lesion appearance and, when uncertain, a biopsy.

[THOUGHT] A 34‑year‑old with multiple, bilateral, skin‑colored, flat‑topped papules confined to the lower eyelid/periorbital region with gradual onset and progressive growth over several years. This anatomic distribution (lower eyelids), multiplicity, symmetry, chronic slow course and morphology strongly favor syringomas — benign eccrine sweat‑duct tumors that classically present in young adults as numerous small (typically 1–3 mm) skin‑colored to yellowish papules around the lower eyelids. Xanthelasma would more often be yellowish, plaque‑like and medially located and is associated with lipid abnormalities (lipids here reported normal). Milia are white, superficial keratin cysts and are usually dome‑shaped rather than flat‑topped. Hidrocystomas are translucent cystic lesions, usually dome‑shaped. Lichen planus on the face is uncommon and usually violaceous/pruritic with other mucocutaneous signs.
